name: Isaiah
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text), checked against the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran Cave 1 (1QIsa-a), copied about 125 BC and preserving the whole book, against the second, fragmentary Isaiah scroll from the same cave (1QIsa-b, 1Q8), whose text stands very close to the Masoretic Text, and against the Septuagint (Old Greek). Scroll readings were checked against Martin Abegg’s transcriptions (as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset); readings that could not be confirmed there are marked “reported.” Septuagint readings were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Significant differences are footnoted; the scrolls’ many differences of spelling are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is rendered “Yahweh of Armies”; see the note at 1:9. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; English 9:1 is Hebrew 8:23, so English 9:2–21 is Hebrew 9:1–20, and English 64:1 is Hebrew 63:19b, so English 64:2–12 is Hebrew 64:1–11.

verses.text: The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.{a}

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth,
for Yahweh has spoken:
“I have nourished and brought up children,
and they have rebelled against me.

The ox knows his owner,
and the donkey the manger of its lord;
Israel has not known,
my people have not understood.”

Ah, sinful nation,
a people heavy with iniquity,
offspring of evildoers,
children who deal corruptly!
They have forsaken Yahweh,
they have despised the Holy One of Israel,
they have turned away backward.{b}

Why will you still be struck,
that you revolt more and more?
The whole head is sick,
and the whole heart faint.

From the sole of the foot even to the head
there is no soundness in it,
but wounds and bruises and fresh sores;
they have not been pressed out, nor bound up,
nor softened with oil.

“What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” says Yahweh.
“I have had my fill of burnt offerings of rams
and the fat of fed beasts;
and I take no delight in the blood of bulls,
or of lambs, or of he-goats.

When you come to appear before me,
who has required this from your hand,
to trample my courts?

Bring no more vain offerings;
incense is an abomination to me.
New moon and sabbath, the calling of assemblies—
I cannot endure iniquity along with the solemn meeting.

If you consent and listen,
the best of the land you shall eat;

How the faithful city has become a harlot!
She that was full of justice!
Righteousness lodged in her,
but now murderers.

Your silver has become dross,
your wine mixed with water.

Your princes are rebels
and companions of thieves.
Every one loves a bribe
and runs after rewards.
They do not judge the fatherless,
and the cause of the widow does not come to them.

Therefore says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
the Mighty One of Israel:{j}
“Ah, I will ease myself of my adversaries,
and avenge myself on my enemies.

And I will restore your judges as at the first,
and your counselors as at the beginning.
Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness,
the faithful city.”

Zion shall be redeemed with justice,
and her returning ones with righteousness.{l}

But the crushing of transgressors and sinners shall be together,
and those who forsake Yahweh shall be consumed.

For they shall be ashamed of the oaks which you desired,
and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen.{m}

For you shall be as an oak whose leaf withers,
and as a garden that has no water.

notes.text: Isaiah, Hebrew Yesha‘yahu, “Yahweh is salvation”; Amoz, “strong” (not the prophet Amos, a different name in Hebrew). Uzziah, “my strength is Yahweh”; Jotham, “Yahweh is perfect”; Ahaz, “he has grasped”; Hezekiah, “Yahweh strengthens.” Their reigns span about 790–686 BC; Uzziah died about 740 BC (6:1). Judah, perhaps “praised”; Jerusalem, perhaps “foundation of Shalem (peace).”
The Holy One of Israel, Isaiah’s characteristic title for God (about twenty-five times in the book). Israel, “God strives” or “he strives with God.”
Hebrew “as the overthrow of strangers”; some propose “as the overthrow of Sodom” (sedom for zarim), compare verses 9–10. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) adds “upon it.”
Zion, the hill of Jerusalem, meaning uncertain (perhaps “fortress”); “daughter of Zion” personifies the city. The cucumber field’s lodge was a watchman’s hut.

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” Tseva’ot means “armies” or “hosts,” whether the armies of Israel, the stars, or the heavenly beings; the title presents Yahweh as commander of every power in heaven and earth. Sodom and Gomorrah, the cities destroyed in Genesis 19; meanings uncertain. Compare Romans 9:29.
Or “instruction” (torah), here prophetic teaching.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “your fingers with iniquity” (compare 59:3).
Or “correct the ruthless”; the Septuagint reads “deliver him that is suffering wrong.” The Hebrew hamots is uncertain.
Or “Though your sins are as scarlet, shall they be white as snow?” The Hebrew may be read as a question.
Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord” (the master). “Mighty One of Israel,” Hebrew ’avir yisra’el; compare Genesis 49:24 (“Mighty One of Jacob”).
Or “purge away … as with potash.” Alloy, or “tin” or “lead,” the base metals separated in refining.
Or “her repentant ones.”
The oaks (or terebinths) and gardens were sites of the fertility cults.
Or “the strong man”; or, with a change of vowels, “your strength” (so the Great Isaiah Scroll, “your strength … your work”).

verses.text: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.

And many peoples shall go and say,
“Come, and let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh,
to the house of the God of Jacob;
and he will teach us from his ways,
and we will walk in his paths.”
For the law shall go out from Zion,
and the word of Yahweh from Jerusalem.{b}

House of Jacob, come,
let us walk in Yahweh’s light.

For you have forsaken your people, the house of Jacob,
because they are filled with customs from the east,
and are soothsayers like the Philistines,
and they strike hands with the children of foreigners.{c}

Their land also is full of silver and gold,
and there is no end of their treasures;
their land also is full of horses,
and there is no end of their chariots.

The lofty looks of man shall be brought low,
and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down,
and Yahweh alone shall be exalted in that day.

and against all the high mountains,
and against all the hills that are lifted up;

and against every lofty tower,
and against every wall made strong;

and against all the ships of Tarshish,
and against all the pleasant craft.{h}
And the idols shall utterly pass away.

And men shall go into the caves of the rocks,
and into the holes of the earth,
from before the terror of Yahweh,
and from the splendor of his majesty,
when he arises to shake the earth with terror.

In that day men shall cast away their idols of silver
and their idols of gold,
which they made for themselves to worship,
to the moles and to the bats;{i}

to go into the clefts of the rocks,
and into the crevices of the crags,
from before the terror of Yahweh,
and from the splendor of his majesty,
when he arises to shake the earth with terror.

Stop trusting in man, who has but breath in his nostrils;
for at what is he to be valued?{j}

notes.text: Verses 2–4 appear also, with small differences, at Micah 4:1–3.
Jacob, “he grasps the heel” or “he supplants,” here the people descended from him. Or “instruction.”

Hebrew “they are filled from the east”; perhaps “filled with diviners from the east” (one word may have dropped out). Philistines, the people of the southern coastal plain. “Strike hands,” that is, make pacts or bargains.
Hebrew ’elilim, a scornful word for idols, sounding like ’elohim (“God”) and meaning “nothings” or “worthless things.”
Or “and you cannot raise them up.” The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this last line (“and do not forgive them”) and all of verse 10; the Septuagint has both.
Compare Revelation 6:15–16.
Lebanon, “white,” the snow-capped mountain range north of Israel; Bashan, the fertile highlands east of the Sea of Galilee.

Tarshish, a distant port in the west, perhaps Tartessus in Spain; “ships of Tarshish” were large seagoing ships. “Pleasant craft,” a rare Hebrew word, perhaps “beautiful vessels”; the Septuagint reads “every ship of the sea, and … every display of fine ships.”
Hebrew “to the dig-rats” (lahpor peroth), a word or words of uncertain meaning, probably moles or shrews; the Great Isaiah Scroll writes it as one word.
The Septuagint lacks this verse; the Great Isaiah Scroll has it.

verses.text:
For behold, the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
takes away from Jerusalem and from Judah
support and supply,
all the support of bread,
and all the support of water;{a}

the warrior and the man of battle,
judge and prophet,
diviner and elder,

the commander of fifty and the man held in honor,
the counselor and the one wise in crafts,
and the one skilled in enchantment.

And I will give boys to be their princes,
and capricious ones shall rule over them.{b}

And the people shall oppress one another,
man against man, and each against his neighbor;
the youth shall behave himself proudly against the old man,
and the base against the honorable.

When a man shall take hold of his brother in the house of his father,
saying, “You have a cloak; you be our ruler,
and let this ruin be under your hand”—

The look on their faces testifies against them,
and they declare their sin like Sodom;
they do not hide it.
Woe to their soul!
For they have brought evil upon themselves.

Say of the righteous that it shall be well with him,
for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.

Woe to the wicked man! Evil is his lot;
for the dealing of his own hands shall be rendered to him.{d}

As for my people, children are their oppressors,
and women rule over them.
O my people, those who lead you cause you to err,
and swallow up the way of your paths.{e}

Yahweh stands up to plead,
and stands to judge the peoples.{f}

Yahweh will enter into judgment
with the elders of his people and their princes:
“It is you who have eaten up the vineyard;
the spoil of the poor is in your houses.

What do you mean by crushing my people,
and grinding the face of the poor?”
says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.

Moreover Yahweh said:
“Because the daughters of Zion are proud,
and go about with necks stretched out
and glancing eyes,
tripping along as they walk,
and jingling with their feet;
In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, and the headbands, and the crescents;{h}
the pendants, and the bracelets, and the veils;
the headdresses, and the ankle chains, and the sashes, and the perfume boxes, and the amulets;
the rings, and the nose jewels;
the festal robes, and the mantles, and the shawls, and the purses;
the mirrors, and the fine linen, and the turbans, and the veils.

Your men shall fall by the sword,
and your mighty ones in the war.

And her gates shall lament and mourn;
and she, emptied, shall sit upon the ground.

notes.text: Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord.” “Support and supply,” Hebrew mash‘en umash‘enah, masculine and feminine forms of one word: “every kind of support.”
Or “infants” or “wanton tyranny.” The Hebrew ta‘alulim is uncertain.
Or “to rebel against his glorious presence.”
Hebrew “the dealing of his hands”; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “shall return to him.”
The Septuagint reads “your exactors strip you, and extortioners rule over you,” perhaps taking the Hebrew as nosim (“creditors”) instead of nashim (“women”). “Swallow up,” or “confuse.”
The Septuagint reads “his people”; Hebrew “peoples.”
Or “their foreheads”; the Hebrew poth is uncertain. In verses 17–18 the Great Isaiah Scroll interchanges ’Adonai (“Lord”) and Yahweh, with scribal corrections above the line.
Many of the items in verses 18–23 are rare words whose exact sense is uncertain.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds a word: “for instead of beauty, shame.” “Branding” (ki) may refer to the branding of slaves; some take it as the conjunction “for.”

verses.text:
In that day the sprout of Yahweh shall be for beauty and for glory,
and the fruit of the land for pride and for splendor to the escaped of Israel.{a}
And it shall come to pass that he who is left in Zion and he who remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy, every one who is written for life in Jerusalem,
when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning.{b}

And Yahweh will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there shall be a canopy.{c}
And there shall be a booth for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from storm and from rain.

notes.text: Or “the sprout of Yahweh”; compare 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and Judah” after “Israel.”
Or “of destruction.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “of storm” (sa‘ar for ba‘er).
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the words from “and smoke” in verse 5 through “a shade in the daytime” in verse 6, probably by a copyist’s eye skipping from one similar word to another.

verses.text:
Now I will sing to my well-beloved
a song of my beloved about his vineyard:
My well-beloved had a vineyard
on a very fruitful hill.{a}

“And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah,
judge, I pray you, between me and my vineyard.

What more was there to do for my vineyard,
that I have not done in it?
Why, when I looked for it to yield grapes,
did it yield wild grapes?

And now I will let you know
what I will do to my vineyard:
I will take away its hedge, and it shall be devoured;
I will break down its wall, and it shall be trodden down.

Woe to those who join house to house,
who add field to field,
until there is no room,
and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land!

For ten acres of vineyard shall yield about six gallons,
and six bushels of seed shall yield about half a bushel.”{e}

Woe to those who rise up early in the morning,
that they may follow strong drink;
who tarry late into the night,
till wine inflames them!

And man is bowed down, and each one is brought low,
and the eyes of the lofty are brought low.

But Yahweh of Armies is exalted in justice,
and God the Holy One shows himself holy in righteousness.

Then the lambs shall graze as in their pasture,
and strangers shall eat among the ruins of the fat ones.{g}

Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood,
and sin as with cart ropes;

who say, “Let him make speed, let him hasten his work,
that we may see it;
and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come,
that we may know it!”

Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes,
and prudent in their own sight!

Woe to those who are mighty at drinking wine,
and valiant men at mixing strong drink;

who justify the wicked for a bribe,
and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!

whose arrows are sharp,
and all their bows bent;
their horses’ hoofs are counted like flint,
and their wheels like a whirlwind.

Their roaring shall be like a lioness,
they shall roar like young lions;
they shall growl and lay hold of the prey,
and carry it off, and none shall deliver.

notes.text: Or “the song of my beloved.” Hebrew “on a horn, a son of oil,” that is, a fertile hillside.
Hebrew be’ushim, “stinking things,” that is, rotten or worthless grapes.
A wordplay: “justice” (mishpat) but “bloodshed” (mispah); “righteousness” (tsedaqah) but “a cry” (tse‘aqah), the outcry of the oppressed.
Hebrew “In my ears, Yahweh of Armies”; “has sworn” is supplied (compare 22:14). The Septuagint reads “these things have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.”

Hebrew “ten yokes of vineyard,” the land ten teams of oxen could plow in a day, “shall yield one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield an ephah.” A bath was about 6 gallons (22 liters); a homer about 6 bushels (220 liters); an ephah about 3/5 bushel (22 liters), a tenth of the seed sown.
Sheol, the realm of the dead; the Septuagint reads Hades.
“The fat ones,” that is, the rich. For gerim, “strangers,” some read gedayim, “kids.” The Septuagint reads “lambs shall feed on the waste places of them that are taken away.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and flaming fire” for “and dry grass in the flame.”
This refrain recurs at 9:12, 17, 21; 10:4.

verses.text: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.{a}
Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.{b}
And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
Then I said, “Woe is me, for I am undone! For I am a man unclean of lips, and in the midst of a people unclean of lips I dwell; and the King, Yahweh of Armies, my eyes have seen!”{d}
Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal, which he had taken with tongs from off the altar.
And he touched my mouth with it and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin is atoned for.”
Then I heard the Lord’s voice say, “Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?” And I said, “Here I am! Send me.”

Make fat the heart of this people,
make heavy their ears,
and smear over their eyes;
so that they may not see with their eyes,
nor hear with their ears,
nor their heart understand,
and they turn and be healed.”{e}

Then I said, “Lord, how long?” And he answered:
“Until cities lie waste without inhabitant,
and houses without man,
and the land is utterly desolate,

and Yahweh has removed men far away,
and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land.

And if there is still a tenth in it,
it shall again be burned,
like a terebinth or an oak,
whose stump remains when it is felled.
The holy seed is its stump.”{f}

notes.text: About 740 BC. “The Lord,” Hebrew ’Adonai. “Train,” the skirts of his robe. Compare John 12:41.
Seraphim, “burning ones,” heavenly beings; the word is also used of serpents (14:29; 30:6; Numbers 21:6). “Feet” may be a modest term for the lower body.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Holy, holy” (twice). Compare Revelation 4:8.
Or “I am silenced” or “I am ruined.”

Verses 9–10 are quoted in Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27, largely following the Septuagint, which reads “For the heart of this people has become fat.” In verse 10 the Great Isaiah Scroll reads hashem for hashmen (“make fat”), perhaps a shortened spelling, or “appall,” as some have proposed.

Or “at its felling.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads mushleket, “cast down,” for beshalleket, “at its felling,” and bamah for bam (“in them”); the sense is uncertain. The Septuagint lacks the last line.

verses.text: And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, that Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, but could not prevail against it.{a}
And it was told the house of David, saying, “Syria has settled upon Ephraim.” And his heart and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.{b}
Then Yahweh said to Isaiah, “Go out now to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway to the washers’ field;{c}
and say to him, ‘Be careful and keep still; have no fear, neither let your heart be faint because of these two stubs of smoldering firebrands, at the hot anger of Rezin and Syria and Remaliah’s son.
Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has counseled evil against you, saying,
“Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us break it open for ourselves, and set up a king in the midst of it, the son of Tabeel,”{d}

For the head of Syria is Damascus,
and the head of Damascus is Rezin.
And within sixty-five years
Ephraim shall be shattered from being a people.{f}

And Samaria is the head of Ephraim,
and Remaliah’s son is the head of Samaria.
If you will not hold firm in trust,
surely you will not be held firm.”’”{g}
And Yahweh spoke again to Ahaz, saying,
“Ask a sign of Yahweh your God; ask it either in the depth below or in the height above.”{h}
But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, neither will I put Yahweh to the test.”
And he said, “Listen, house of David! Is it too little for you to tire men out, that you will tire out my God as well?

Butter and honey shall he eat,
when he knows to refuse the evil and choose the good.{j}
For before the child knows to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread shall be forsaken.

Yahweh will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father such days
as have not come from the day when Ephraim broke away from Judah—the king of Assyria.”{k}
And it shall come to pass in that day that Yahweh will whistle for the fly that is in the farthest part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.
And they shall come and shall rest, all of them, in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and upon all thornbushes, and upon all watering places.{l}
In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River—with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet; and it shall also sweep away the beard.{m}
And it shall come to pass in that day that a man shall keep alive a young cow and two sheep;
and it shall come to pass, for the abundance of milk that they give, he shall eat butter; for butter and honey shall every one eat who is left in the midst of the land.
And it shall come to pass in that day that every place where there were a thousand vines, worth about twenty-five pounds of silver, shall become briers and thorns.{n}
With arrows and with bow shall one come there, because all the land shall become briers and thorns.
And as for all the hills that were dug with the hoe, you shall not come there for fear of briers and thorns; but it shall be a place for sending out oxen and for the treading of sheep.

notes.text: Ahaz reigned about 735–715 BC. Rezin, perhaps “delight,” the last king of Aram (Syria) at Damascus; Pekah, “opened (eyes)”; Remaliah, perhaps “Yahweh has adorned.” This is the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734 BC; compare 2 Kings 16:5.
Hebrew Aram, the Aramean kingdom of Damascus. Ephraim, “doubly fruitful,” here the northern kingdom of Israel. “Settled upon,” or “is allied with.” David, “beloved.”
Shear-jashub, “a remnant shall return” (compare 10:21–22). Or “the fuller’s field.” Compare 36:2.
Tabeel, “God is good,” here with a pun on “good for nothing” (tav’al); perhaps an Aramean candidate for the throne.
Hebrew ’Adonai YHWH.

Damascus, the capital of Aram. Samaria (verse 9), the capital of the northern kingdom, fell to Assyria in 722 BC; the sixty-five years may reckon to the resettlement of the land (compare 2 Kings 17:24; Ezra 4:2).
A wordplay: “If you will not be firm (ta’aminu), you shall not be made firm (te’amenu).”
Or “make it deep as Sheol,” reading she’alah as she’olah.

Hebrew ha‘almah, “the young woman,” a girl of marriageable age, unmarried or newly married; it is not the usual Hebrew word for a virgin (betulah), and it does not of itself say whether she is a virgin. Or “is with child and is about to bear a son.” The Septuagint, made about two centuries before Christ, renders the word parthenos, ordinarily “virgin,” and Matthew 1:23 quotes the Septuagint (“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel”) of the birth of Jesus. The second-century Jewish Greek translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion are reported by early Christian writers to have read neanis, “young woman.” Immanuel, ‘immanu ’el, “God is with us” (compare 8:8, 10). “Shall call,” or “you shall call”; the Septuagint reads “you shall call,” and the Great Isaiah Scroll “he shall call” (or “one shall call”). The Great Isaiah Scroll also reads Yahweh for ’Adonai (“the Lord”).
Or “curds and honey,” the food of a land returned to pasture (verse 22). “When he knows,” or “so that he may know.”
Assyria, the great power of upper Mesopotamia, with its capital at Nineveh.
Or “all the pastures.”
The River, the Euphrates. “The hair of the feet,” the body hair; shaving was a mark of humiliation (2 Samuel 10:4).
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms).

verses.text: And Yahweh said to me, “Take a large tablet and write upon it in common characters, ‘For Maher-shalal-hash-baz.’{a}
And I will take for myself faithful witnesses to testify, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah.”{b}
And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then Yahweh said to me, “Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz;{c}
for before the child knows how to cry ‘My father’ and ‘My mother,’ the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be carried away before the king of Assyria.”
And Yahweh spoke to me yet again, saying,
For thus Yahweh spoke to me with a strong hand, and warned me not to walk in the way of this people, saying,{h}

And many shall stumble on it,
and fall and be broken,
and be snared and be taken.”

Bind up the testimony;
seal the law among my disciples.{k}

And I will wait for Yahweh,
who hides his face from the house of Jacob,
and I will look for him.
Behold, I and the children whom Yahweh has given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from Yahweh of Armies, who dwells on Mount Zion.{l}
And when they say to you, “Seek the mediums and the spiritists who chirp and mutter,” is it not to its God that a people should inquire? On behalf of the living, should they inquire of the dead?{m}
To the law and to the testimony! Surely those who do not speak according to this word have no dawn.{n}

And they shall pass through it, hard pressed and hungry; and it shall come to pass that when they are hungry they shall fret themselves, and curse their king and their God, and turn their faces upward;
and they shall look to the earth, and behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish; and into thick darkness they shall be thrust.{o}

notes.text: Hebrew “with the stylus of a man,” that is, in ordinary script. Maher-shalal-hash-baz, “the spoil speeds, the prey hastens,” foretelling the plundering of Damascus and Samaria (verse 4).

Uriah, “Yahweh is my light,” the priest of 2 Kings 16:10–16; Zechariah, “Yahweh remembers”; Jeberechiah, “Yahweh blesses.” “I will take,” so the Hebrew; the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read imperatives (“take for me” / “make … witnesses”).
The prophetess, probably Isaiah’s wife.
Shiloah, “sent,” the gentle stream from the Gihon spring (compare Siloam, John 9:7), a symbol of the quiet rule of the house of David. “Rejoices in,” the sense of the Hebrew is uncertain.
Immanuel, “God is with us”; see 7:14.
The Septuagint reads “Know, O nations”; some read “Be joined together” for “Be broken.” The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the last line.
Hebrew ‘immanu ’el, “God is with us,” the name of 7:14.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and he turned me aside from walking” for “and warned me.”
Or “what they reverence.” Compare 1 Peter 3:14–15.
Compare Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8.
Or “instruction” (torah), here Isaiah’s teaching.
Compare Hebrews 2:13.
Hebrew ’ovot and yidd‘onim, those who consulted ghosts and the spirits of the dead; compare Leviticus 19:31; 1 Samuel 28.
Or “surely they shall speak according to this word, for which there is no dawn.” The Hebrew is difficult.
In the Hebrew text 8:23 begins with the first line of English 9:1.

verses.text: But there shall be no gloom for her who was in distress. In the former time he brought contempt upon the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.{a}

For the yoke of his burden,
and the bar across his shoulder,
the rod of his taskmaster,
you have broken as on the day of Midian.{d}

For every boot of the warrior that tramped in the tumult,
and every cloak rolled in blood,
shall be for burning, food for the fire.

Of the increase of his rule and of peace
there shall be no end,
upon the throne of David and over his kingdom,
to establish it and to uphold it
with justice and with righteousness
from now on and forever.
The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will do this.{f}

A word the Lord sent into Jacob,
and it has fallen upon Israel;{g}

and all the people shall know it,
Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria,
who say in pride and in arrogance of heart:

So Yahweh raises the foes of Rezin against him,
and spurs on his enemies,

Yet the people have not turned to him who struck them,
nor have they sought Yahweh of Armies.

So Yahweh cuts off from Israel head and tail,
palm branch and reed, in one day—

the elder and the man of rank, he is the head;
and the prophet who teaches lies, he is the tail.

For those who lead this people lead them astray,
and those who are led by them are swallowed up.{j}

Manasseh Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh,
and together they are against Judah.
For all this his anger has not turned back,
and his hand is stretched out still.{n}

notes.text: This verse is 8:23 in the Hebrew, and English 9:2–21 are Hebrew 9:1–20. Zebulun, “honor” or “dwelling”; Naphtali, “my wrestling”; Galilee, “circle” or “district,” here the region of the nations around Israel’s north. Or “Galilee of the Gentiles.” Verses 1–2 are quoted in Matthew 4:15–16 of the ministry of Jesus in Galilee.
Or “deep darkness.”

The Hebrew written text (ketiv) reads “you have not made great its joy”; the text as traditionally read aloud (qere) has “to it” (lo) for “not” (lo’), as here. The Great Isaiah Scroll has the written form, “not.”
Midian, “strife”; the day of Gideon’s victory over Midian (Judges 7). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Madim.”

Hebrew pele’ yo‘ets, ’el gibbor, ’avi‘ad, sar shalom; or “a Wonder of a Counselor,” “God the Warrior” (compare 10:21, where ’el gibbor is God himself), “Father forever.” Some, following medieval Jewish interpretation, take the long name as a sentence describing God who gives the child (“the Wonderful Counselor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father, calls him Prince of Peace”). The Septuagint reads “and his name is called the Messenger of great counsel, for I will bring peace upon the princes.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Prince of the peace” and “and he called.” In the Hebrew this is 9:5.

In the traditional Hebrew text the first word (lemarbeh, “of the increase”) is written with a final form of the letter mem in the middle of the word, a feature long discussed by interpreters; the Great Isaiah Scroll writes it normally. David, “beloved.”
The Septuagint reads “The Lord has sent death” (dever, “pestilence,” for davar, “word”).
Or “sycamore figs,” a common, cheap timber.
Hebrew Aram from the front and the Philistines from behind, that is, east and west. The Septuagint reads “Syria from the rising of the sun, and the Greeks from the setting of the sun.” Compare 5:25.
Or “confused.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “does not spare” (yahmol for yismah).
Or “is shaken” or “burned up”; the Hebrew ne‘tam is uncertain.
Or, with some, “the flesh of his neighbor” (re‘o for zero‘o). Manasseh, “causing to forget”; Ephraim, “doubly fruitful,” the two great tribes of the northern kingdom.

verses.text:
Woe to those who decree unjust decrees,
and the writers who keep writing oppression,

to turn aside the needy from justice,
and to rob the poor of my people of their right,
so that widows become their spoil,
and they plunder the fatherless!

What will you do on the day of punishment,
and in the ruin that comes from afar?
To whom will you flee for help,
and where will you leave your wealth?{a}

Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners,
or to fall among the slain.
For all this his anger has not turned back,
and his hand is stretched out still.{b}

Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger!
The staff in their hand is my fury.{c}

Against a godless nation I send him,
and against the people of my wrath I command him,
to take spoil and to seize plunder,
and to trample them like the mud of the streets.

But this is not what he means,
nor is it what his heart devises;
but to destroy is in his heart,
and to cut off many nations.

For he says:
“Are my princes not every one of them kings?

As my hand has reached the kingdoms of the idols,
whose carved images were more than those of Jerusalem and of Samaria,

shall I not do to Jerusalem and her images
as I have done to Samaria and her idols?”

And it shall come to pass, when the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, that I will punish the fruit of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria, and the boasting of his haughty eyes.{e}

Shall the axe boast itself over him who hews with it?
Shall the saw magnify itself against him who wields it?
As if a rod should wield those who lift it,
or as if a staff should lift him who is not wood!{g}

And the Light of Israel shall become a fire,
and his Holy One a flame;
and it shall burn and devour
his thorns and his briers in one day.

And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few,
so that a child could write them down.

And it shall come to pass in that day that the remnant of Israel, and the survivors of the house of Jacob, shall no more lean upon him who struck them, but shall lean upon Yahweh, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.

A remnant shall return, the remnant of Jacob,
to the Mighty God.{j}

For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea,
only a remnant of them shall return.
Destruction is decreed,
overflowing with righteousness.{k}

For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, as decreed,
in the midst of all the land.{l}
Therefore thus says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies: “O my people who dwell in Zion, do not be afraid of Assyria, when he strikes you with the rod and lifts up his staff against you as Egypt did.{m}
For in a very little while the indignation will come to an end, and my anger will turn to their destruction.
And Yahweh of Armies will wield a whip against him, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb; and his staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it up as he did in Egypt.{n}
And it shall come to pass in that day that his burden shall depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke shall be broken because of fatness.”{o}

Madmenah is in flight;
the inhabitants of Gebim flee for refuge.{s}

Behold, the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
will lop the boughs with terrifying power;
and the tall of stature shall be hewn down,
and the lofty shall be brought low.

And he will cut down the thickets of the forest with iron,
and Lebanon shall fall by a Mighty One.{u}

notes.text: Hebrew “your glory.”
Or “Without me they shall crouch.” The Hebrew is uncertain. See 5:25.
Or “Ah, Assyria.” Assyria’s king is the tool of God’s judgment (verses 5–19).
Calno (Calneh), Carchemish (on the Euphrates), Hamath, and Arpad were cities of Syria and northern Mesopotamia taken by Assyria about 740–717 BC.
The Lord, here ’Adonai.
Or “like a bull.” “Treasures,” or “stores”; the Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this word.
Or “as if a rod should wave him who lifts it.”
Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord.”
Or “as when a standard-bearer faints”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Hebrew she’ar yashuv, the name of Isaiah’s son (7:3). Hebrew ’el gibbor, as in 9:6.
Verses 22–23 are quoted in Romans 9:27–28 from the Septuagint (“a remnant of them shall be saved”).
Or “in the midst of all the earth.”
Egypt, Hebrew Mitsrayim, the land of Israel’s first bondage.
Oreb, “raven,” the Midianite prince killed at the rock that bore his name (Judges 7:25).

Hebrew “from before oil” or “from before fatness,” perhaps meaning the ox has grown too fat for its yoke; many emend to “he has gone up from Samaria” or “from Rimmon.” The verse division is uncertain; the last words may begin verse 28.
Verses 28–32 trace an army’s advance on Jerusalem from the north. Aiath, probably Ai, “ruin”; Migron, perhaps “precipice”; Michmash, “hidden place.”
Geba and Gibeah, both “hill”; Ramah, “height.” Saul, “asked for,” Israel’s first king.
Gallim, “heaps”; Laishah, “lion”; Anathoth, the priestly town of Jeremiah. “Answer her,” reading ‘aniha; Hebrew ‘aniyyah, “poor.”
Madmenah, “dung heap”; Gebim, “cisterns” or “trenches.”
Nob, the priests’ town (1 Samuel 21–22), within sight of Jerusalem. Hebrew ketiv “the house of the daughter of Zion”; the Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “house.”
Or “by the Mighty One,” or “by a majestic one” (’addir). Lebanon here stands for the Assyrian army, as the forest image continues.

verses.text:
And a shoot shall come out from the stock of Jesse,
and a branch out of his roots shall be fruitful.{a}

And the Spirit of Yahweh shall rest upon him,
the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,
the Spirit of counsel and might,
the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.{b}

And righteousness shall be the sash about his waist,
and faithfulness the sash about his hips.

And the suckling child shall play by the cobra’s hole,
and on the viper’s nest the weaned child shall lay his hand.
And it shall come to pass in that day that the root of Jesse, who stands for a banner of the peoples—to him the nations shall seek, and his place of rest shall be glorious.{e}

And it shall come to pass in that day that the Lord will set his hand a second time to recover the remnant of his people that remains, from Assyria and from Egypt, from Pathros and from Cush, from Elam and from Shinar, from Hamath and from the coastlands of the sea.{f}

And he will raise a banner for the nations,
and will gather the outcasts of Israel,
and assemble the scattered of Judah
from the four corners of the earth.

And the jealousy of Ephraim shall depart,
and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off;
Ephraim shall not envy Judah,
and Judah shall not harass Ephraim.

And there shall be a highway for the remnant of his people
that remains from Assyria,
as there was for Israel
on the day when they came up from the land of Egypt.

notes.text: Jesse, David’s father (1 Samuel 16); the name’s meaning is uncertain, perhaps “Yahweh exists” or “gift.” “Branch,” Hebrew netser; compare Matthew 2:23. The Septuagint reads “a rod … and a blossom shall come up from his root.”
The Septuagint adds “godliness” after “knowledge” and puts “the fear of God” in verse 3, giving the seven gifts of later Christian tradition.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and by the breath of his lips the wicked shall be put to death.” Compare 2 Thessalonians 2:8.
The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read “shall graze” for “and the fatling”; compare 65:25.
Quoted in Romans 15:12 from the Septuagint (“he who rises to rule the nations; in him shall the nations hope”).
Pathros, Upper (southern) Egypt; Cush, the Nile lands south of Egypt (Nubia); Elam, southwest Iran; Shinar, Babylonia; Hamath, in Syria. The Lord, here ’Adonai.
Edom, “red,” south and east of the Dead Sea; Moab, east of the Dead Sea; Ammon, east of the Jordan, around modern Amman.
Or “will dry up” (some read hehrib for heherim). The River, the Euphrates. “Scorching,” the Hebrew word is uncertain.

verses.text:
And with joy you shall draw water
from the springs of salvation.

Sing to Yahweh, for he has done excellent things;
let it be known through all the earth.{c}

Cry out and shout, you who dwell in Zion,
for the Holy One of Israel is great among you.”{d}

notes.text: “You” is singular here; in verse 4 it is plural. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and turned away.”
Yah, a short form of the divine name; compare Exodus 15:2; Psalm 118:14. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “God, God (’el ’el) is my salvation.”
Following the qere (muda‘at); the ketiv has another passive form of the same verb. The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the word rendered “let it be known.”
Or “O inhabitress of Zion,” a feminine form for the city’s people.
